item.title: How to Find the Best Deals Over Labor Day and Beyond
item.description:
Travel usually favors those who plan ahead with the best prices. Think of airfares, which tend to spike close to departure, or cruise rates that rise as ships fill.

But not every cost can be reduced with advance planning. According to the booking site Hotels.com, last-minute bookers saved an average of 23 percent over those who booked four or more months ahead. On average, the best time to capture savings, it said, is eight to 14 days out.

That’s great news for those just waking up to the fact that Labor Day is just a few weeks away.

Most of the following budget strategies rest on one key principle: flexibility — whether you are traveling on Labor Day weekend or beyond.

To save on airfares, follow the deal, not the destination.

Kayak’s new Monthly Flight Deal Tracker rounds up the lowest average round-trip fares from more than 30 American airports. Users can pick a region to see domestic and international fare deals from cities in the area. For example, the tracker recently showed a round-trip August flight from Boston to Riga, Latvia, for $558, which it said was down 35 percent compared with July’s average price. It also calls out the cheapest domestic route in the country — currently Atlanta to Jacksonville, Fla., averaging $55 round trip.

Skyscanner users can make their destination “everywhere,” which brings up the cheapest flights across the world from a given airport.

Expedia will track ticket prices and tell you when to book based on historical data if you join its free One Key rewards program. After you’ve booked, new A.I.-based apps will monitor the fare and, if it drops, request a refund from the airline, usually for a fee.

Keep in mind that Labor Day weekend airfares are highest if you leave on Friday, Sept. 4, and return on Monday. A recent check on Kayak for nonstop round-trip fares between New York and Portland, Maine, over those dates started at around $500. If you returned on Tuesday, Sept. 8, you’d save $50. And if you shifted the trip forward to fly on less busy days — out Wednesday, returning Saturday — round trips started at around $240.

Don’t wait to use loyalty points. What 50,000 miles bought yesterday might require 80,000 tomorrow.

Airlines have made it easier to spend points, even at the last minute.

“In the old days, airlines restricted award seats, and it could be tough to find a flight with miles late in the game when demand was high and many seats were already booked,” said Julian Kheel, the founder and chief executive of Points Path, a service that compares prices in cash and miles and tells you which is the better deal. “However,” he said, “today, most airlines have seats available with points and miles so long as they’re available with cash.”

As with any booking, play with the dates and destinations to get the best return.

The popularity of road trips continues through Labor Day. Bookings across the Northeast with Turo, the car-sharing platform for rentals, are up 18 percent over the 2025 long weekend.

For families and groups, renting a car can be cheaper — and for spontaneous travelers, easier to plan — than flying. To encourage those concerned about high gas prices, Hertz is offering 10 percent off electric and hybrid rentals through September.

Booking a week or two out is a good time to find a deal on an R.V. rental through Outdoorsy, the platform for peer-to-peer R.V. rentals. From now through September, including Labor Day weekend, travelers can book with the code SAVESUMMER150 to get $150 off trips through the end of November.

For families and groups, short-term rentals can offer savings over multiple hotel rooms. Hotels also offer enticements such as restaurant and bar credits, free parking and spa discounts.

To make an apples-to-apples comparison, consider the value of any complimentary or discounted amenities when evaluating a deal beside the bottom-line price of a rental, which should include administrative and cleaning fees.

An online travel agency or a booking platform can be a good place to start an accommodations search. But the best deals are usually offered from the property itself, whether a hotel or a rental.

“A lot of independent hotels will offer incentives to book directly, such as waiving fees or offering free amenities,” said Stuart Butler, the president of Visit Myrtle Beach and host of the travel marketing podcast “Destination Discourse.”

The Lodge at Schroon Lake in New York’s Adirondack Mountains, for example, will match any price found at an online agency and take an additional 10 percent off.

“Even if you start your search on a third-party site, it’s always worth checking directly before you book,” said Chuck Donnelly, the general manager of the resort.

The same strategy applies to short-term rentals. Platforms such as Savvy offer Airbnb-like searches and then send travelers directly to the owner to book, saving administration and service fees.

Travelers searching Airbnb and Vrbo can look for clues in a listing — such as a name for the property — and use Google to see if it has its own website that accepts direct bookings.

Booking an all-inclusive hotel or package tends to rein in spending, and their appeal is growing. Hotels.com said searches for all-inclusive deals were up 50 percent in its 2026 report.

Las Vegas has long offered attractive overnight rates, only to hit bargain seekers with high costs for shows and dining. But this year, even Vegas resorts are offering all-inclusive packages. For example, MGM Resorts’ Luxor and Excalibur properties have an all-inclusive deal, including during Labor Day, starting at $330 for two people for two nights. The price includes three meals a day, two tickets to a show at an MGM resort, rides on the roller coaster at its New York-New York resort and $25 in gaming credits. The company said it represented savings of at least $400 over booking separately.

Travel companies regularly offer sales, which can be fleeting. To catch one, sign up for emails or newsletters, or follow the businesses on social media.

“Our email subscribers are often the first to hear about flash sales,” said Mr. Donnelly of the Lodge at Schroon Lake.

With some schools starting in August, family-friendly destinations like Hawaii and Myrtle Beach, S.C., tend to have a dip in traffic, making it a good time to look for offers. In Myrtle Beach, a destination-wide hotel sale is offering four nights for the price of three through year-end; over Labor Day weekend, the deal recently included more than 40 hotels under $200 a night, 29 of them under $100 a night.

If you’re flexible on where you go, Booking.com’s Getaway Deals page can be a good source of inspiration, with hotel discounts usually starting at 15 percent. Vrbo maintains a last-minute deals page devoted to vacation rental discounts, usually between 5 and 20 percent.

Finding a campsite over Labor Day weekend in a national park and popular state parks can be tough. Consider national forests, where the Forest Service often maintains basic cabins and even decommissioned fire tower lookouts for overnight rentals.

Even these can be booked solid during peak periods when platforms like Hipcamp and the Dyrt offer expanded outdoor options. They have made it easier to find alternative camping destinations by offering rentals ranging from basic camp sites in public recreational areas to yurts, cabins and R.V. rentals on private lands, usually at affordable rates.

For example, over Labor Day weekend near Yosemite National Park, the Dyrt recently showed a $25 campsite in the Stanislaus National Forest, and Hipcamp offered a private room on an area ranch for $138 a night.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: How the $32 Trillion Treasury Market Influences the Economy
item.description:
Investors are worried about the amount of debt the government has piled up, and bond yields are one key indicator showing this.

Yields, or interest rates, on bonds can rise when investors rush to sell them. And they’re selling them at a rapid clip. Yields on the 30-year Treasury rose above 5.3 percent — a nearly two-decade high — fueled by anxiety over the war in Iran, inflation, unstable government deficits and rampant spending on artificial intelligence.

The nearly $32 trillion market for U.S. government bonds, called the Treasury market, offers a clear signal of where the economy may be headed. Yields on bonds tend to set the temperature for other interest rates, including mortgages and auto loans. They can affect everything from student loans to the housing market.

Here’s a guide to understanding what is happening with Treasury yields right now, and why it matters.

First the basics.

A bond is a form of debt, which means that when it is issued, someone is borrowing money and someone else is lending it. In the U.S. government bond market, the borrower is the federal government and the bonds are called Treasuries. Other governments do this, too: In Britain, they’re called gilts, and in Japan, they’re known as J.G.B.s, which stands for Japanese government bonds.

The lender is the bond investor, who expects to be paid interest on the investment. That’s a key difference between a bond and other assets that people buy or trade, like stocks: The bond’s yield is the total annual return someone can expect to earn from it. (A bond’s yield rises as its price falls, and vice versa.)

Similar to the rate a homeowner pays on a mortgage, a bond yield reflects a variety of factors: when the debt will be repaid, the risk that it won’t be, the investor’s view on whether earnings on the loan will be more worthwhile than other investments — like stocks and cryptocurrencies.

When an investor owns a Treasury bond until it matures, the return the investor will receive is fixed, but because government bonds are publicly traded, their value can rise or fall just like a stock price, and that means yields move higher or lower, too. Higher yields mean investors are demanding a higher return to make the investment worth it to them.

Even within the world of Treasuries, there is a lot of variety. The United States issues debt with a range of “maturities” — a term that refers to when it has to be paid back — from four-week Treasury bills to the 30-year Treasury bond.

Often, it’s the 10-year Treasury note that gets a lot of attention. It has been climbing since late February, when the yield sat at 3.96 percent. Although the rise began reversing in April and then again in May, the yield began rocketing back up by the end of June. It’s currently 4.66 percent.

The rise has been less steep than previous runs, like when President Trump announced sweeping tariffs in April last year. But investors are aware of a cocktail of forces unlikely to rein in climbing yields.

The flip-flopping on a peace deal in Iran continues to rock oil markets, which in turn adds worries over inflation numbers and affordability. Pair that with rampant spending by tech companies on A.I., which has left some analysts guessing that the hype has drawn investors away from bonds and others saying the enthusiasm has pumped up growth and inflation expectations.

The Treasury buyer “is now much more price sensitive, meaning investors are demanding a higher yield to absorb both government and corporate issuance,” Jason Goldberg, a Barclays analyst, wrote in a note.

Some analysts said that a recent pullback in the equity market is a sign stock investors are growing more worried about bond yields, too.

Typically, bond prices and stocks move inversely. When stocks fall, investors move to a safer investment, like government bonds, to protect from losses. That negative correlation persisted for the first two decades of the 21st century, but has recently flipped. The correlation, now positive, is at its highest level since the 1990s, Bank of America analysts said in a research note on Wednesday.

That flipped correlation means bonds don’t hedge losses the same way they used to, because when stocks fall, so do bond prices.

“Investors are no longer willing to pay the same premium for an asset class that offers lower hedging utility,” the Bank of America analysts wrote.

One reason the 10-year yield gets so much attention is that it is the starting point from which lenders determine mortgage rates, which means that as it rises, taking out a loan to buy a home becomes more expensive.

As of Wednesday, the average interest rate on a 30-year mortgage was 6.67 percent, up from roughly 6 percent earlier in the year, according to data from Freddie Mac.

Because Treasuries are issued in varying maturities, each set offers predictions for what will happen in the economy at different time periods.

Typically, the longer the horizon for an investment, the more bond investors expect to be paid in interest. (We have more certainty about how things will go over the next three months than we do about the next decade.)

So the yield on a 10-year Treasury note is usually higher than the yield on one that matures in just a few months or a couple of years. When that relationship reverses during periods of increased economic anxiety, as it did in 2022, it is used as a recession indicator, because the risk in the near term eclipses the long-term risk.

Although yields have room to rise “modestly higher,” the uptick isn’t yet a cause for alarms about buyer strikes or a dysfunctional market, according to a Wednesday note by LPL Financial’s chief fixed income strategist, Lawrence Gillum.

The demand for bonds at last week’s three-, 10- and 30-year auctions was decent, Mr. Gillum said.

“The market is absorbing the paper,” he said. “That is the mechanism we would expect in a normalization: Higher yields recruit buyers. In a crisis, higher yields chase them away.”
